readings.title: The Wolf and the Lamb
readings.challenge: Notice that the Lamb answers each of the Wolf’s complaints, and that the answers change nothing.
readings.focus: A strong animal pretends to need a reason for something he has already decided to do.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Lambikin is a pet name for the Lamb. A tyrant is someone who uses power cruelly. Jacobs prints the Wolf’s growl in large letters, WARRA WARRA; read it as a growl.
readings.contentNote: The Wolf kills and eats the Lamb at the end of the fable.

excerpt.locator: “The Wolf and the Lamb,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “Once upon a time a Wolf was lapping at a spring on a hillside, when, looking up, what…”; closes ““Any excuse will serve a tyrant.””.

questions.prompt: What does the Wolf think to himself before he says anything to the Lamb?
facilitatorNotes: “There’s my supper”: he has already decided to eat her and only wants an excuse. Ask whether his questions to the Lamb are real questions.
evidence: if only I can find some excuse to seize it

questions.prompt: How does the Lamb prove she cannot have muddied the Wolf’s water?
facilitatorNotes: The stream runs downhill from the Wolf to the Lamb, so mud from her could not reach him. A tilted hand or a tray of water shows it.
evidence: it runs down from you to me

questions.prompt: When the Lamb answers his second complaint too, what does the Wolf say? What does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: “I don’t care” and “if it was not you it was your father”: the truth never mattered to him. Some children will say he gave up pretending; both readings fit.
evidence: if it was not you it was your father

questions.prompt: The Lamb says the moral herself. What does it mean, and who needs to hear it?
facilitatorNotes: A bully will find some excuse whatever you say. Some children hear a warning to watch out for such excuses; others hear that the Lamb was not to blame. Either fits the words.
evidence: Any excuse will serve a tyrant.

readings.title: The Lion’s Share
readings.challenge: Count the Lion’s four reasons and notice what is different about the last one.
readings.focus: A strong leader calls it fairness when he takes everything.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A stag is a male deer. To quarter something is to cut it into four parts. An arbiter is a judge who settles an argument, and the spoil is what is won and shared out.
readings.contentNote: The animals kill a stag and cut it up to share.

excerpt.locator: “The Lion’s Share,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “The Lion went once a-hunting along with the Fox, the Jackal, and the Wolf. They hunted…”; closes ““You may share the labours of the great, but you will not share the spoil.””.

questions.prompt: Into how many parts do the animals cut the Stag, and how many does the Lion keep?
facilitatorNotes: Four parts, and he keeps all four. Four hunters and four quarters would have made one each, which is what makes his speech so unfair.
evidence: cut it into four parts
The first quarter is for me

questions.prompt: The Lion gives a reason for the first three quarters. What does he give instead of a reason for the last one?
facilitatorNotes: A dare: anyone who touches it will have to face him. A threat is not a reason, though he says it as if it were.
evidence: I should like to see which of you will dare to lay a paw upon it

questions.prompt: Why does the Fox speak only “in a low growl” as he walks away?
facilitatorNotes: He is afraid of the Lion and too weak to argue. Some children will call him wise to keep quiet; others will say he is unhappy but powerless. Both fit his tail “between his legs.”
evidence: he spoke in a low growl
with his tail between his legs

readings.title: The Wolf and the Crane
readings.challenge: Notice a promise made in trouble, and what happens to it when the trouble is over.
readings.focus: The Wolf turns the Crane’s danger into a “reward.”
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A crane is a tall bird with a long neck and a long, pointed beak. Gorging is eating greedily. Gratitude is being thankful and showing it.

excerpt.locator: “The Wolf and the Crane,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Wolf had been gorging on an animal he had killed, when suddenly a small bone in the…”; closes “Gratitude and greed go not together.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Wolf promise while the bone is stuck in his throat?
facilitatorNotes: Anything at all. Ask the child to say his words the way someone in pain would.
evidence: I would give anything

questions.prompt: How does the Crane get the bone out? Why is that brave?
facilitatorNotes: It puts its long neck right down the Wolf’s throat, between his teeth. Only the Crane’s shape could do it, and only a trusting bird would try.
evidence: put its long neck down the Wolf’s throat

questions.prompt: The Wolf says the Crane’s reward is getting its head out safely. Is that a reward?
facilitatorNotes: No: it is a threat dressed up as a gift, and his grin “showed his teeth.” Some children may say the Crane was simply lucky; ask what the Wolf could have given instead.
evidence: The Wolf grinned and showed his teeth
that ought to be reward enough for you

questions.prompt: The moral says gratitude and greed do not go together. Where do you see greed in this fable?
facilitatorNotes: At the start he was “gorging,” and at the end he keeps the promised reward. The fable opens and closes on the same greed.
evidence: A Wolf had been gorging
Gratitude and greed go not together.

readings.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
readings.challenge: Compare two homes and two meals, and decide what each mouse cares about most.
readings.focus: A plain life in peace is weighed against a rich life in fear.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Fare means food. Mastiffs are very big, heavy dogs. Ale is a kind of beer.

excerpt.locator: “The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “Now you must know that a Town Mouse once upon a time went on a visit to his cousin in the…”; closes ““Better beans and bacon in peace than cakes and ale in fear.””.

questions.prompt: What food does the Country Mouse offer, and how does he offer it?
facilitatorNotes: Beans and bacon, cheese and bread, offered “freely” and with a hearty welcome. The food is plain but the welcome is warm.
evidence: Beans and bacon, cheese and bread, were all he had to offer, but he offered them freely.

questions.prompt: How does the Town Mouse show what he thinks of the country?
facilitatorNotes: He turns up his nose at the food and says he will show his cousin “how to live,” as if country life were not really living.
evidence: turned up his long nose at this country fare
come you with me and I will show you how to live

questions.prompt: The Country Mouse calls the barking “music at my dinner.” Is he joking? What does he mean?
facilitatorNotes: He uses a polite, joking word for a frightening noise: he does not want danger with his meal. Children may hear him as calm, or as scared and pretending not to be.
evidence: I do not like that music at my dinner.

questions.prompt: Which mouse would you rather be? Use the last line to explain the Country Mouse’s choice.
facilitatorNotes: “Better beans and bacon in peace than cakes and ale in fear.” A child who chooses the town for the cakes is welcome to, as long as they weigh the mastiffs too.
evidence: Better beans and bacon in peace than cakes and ale in fear.

readings.title: The Fox and the Crow
readings.challenge: Listen for every compliment the Fox pays, and keep in mind what he really wants.
readings.focus: Praise used as a trick.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Master Reynard is an old storybook name for a fox. To surpass is to be better than. A flatterer praises you to get something from you. In the closing rhyme, “by stealth” means secretly and “wit” means good sense.

excerpt.locator: “The Fox and the Crow,” the whole fable with its moral and closing rhyme; opens “A Fox once saw a Crow fly off with a piece of cheese in its beak and settle on a branch…”; closes “The Flatter doth rob by stealth, His victim, both of Wit and Wealth.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Fox want, and what does he say to himself before he speaks to the Crow?
facilitatorNotes: The cheese. “That’s for me, as I am a Fox”: he has a plan before he says a word.
evidence: That’s for me, as I am a Fox

questions.prompt: Name the Fox’s compliments. Which one is the trap?
facilitatorNotes: Glossy feathers, bright eye, and a fine voice. The voice is the trap, because singing means opening her beak.
evidence: how glossy your feathers; how bright your eye
let me hear but one song from you

questions.prompt: The Fox gives the Crow advice “in exchange for your cheese.” Is that a fair trade?
facilitatorNotes: He is laughing at her; she did not choose the trade. Some children will say the advice really is worth having; ask whether she would have paid that price on purpose.
evidence: In exchange for your cheese I will give you a piece of advice for the future

questions.prompt: The rhyme says a flatterer robs his victim of “Wit and Wealth.” What did the Crow lose of each?
facilitatorNotes: Wealth is the cheese; wit is her good sense, lost when she believed the praise. Accept other answers that match the two words to something in the story.
evidence: His victim, both of Wit and Wealth.

readings.title: The Ass and the Lapdog
readings.challenge: Work out why something charming from one animal goes wrong from another.
readings.focus: Copying someone else’s way of being loved can backfire.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. An ass is a donkey, and a lapdog is a small pet dog that sits on laps. A halter is a rope around an animal’s head. Beasts of burden are animals that carry loads.
readings.contentNote: The servants drive the donkey off with sticks and pitchforks.

excerpt.locator: “The Ass and the Lapdog,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Farmer one day came to the stables to see to his beasts of burden: among them was his…”; closes “Clumsy jesting is no joke.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Lapdog do that pleases the Farmer?
facilitatorNotes: Dances, licks his hand, frisks about, and lies in his lap. Let the child act out one of them.
evidence: danced about and licked his hand
jumped into his master’s lap

questions.prompt: The Ass was already the Farmer’s favourite. Why do you think he copies the Lapdog?
facilitatorNotes: He was well fed and often carried his master, yet he wants the same petting; perhaps he is jealous. Ask whether he needed to change at all.
evidence: his favourite Ass, that was always well fed and often carried his master

questions.prompt: Why does the same thing go so wrong when the Ass does it?
facilitatorNotes: He is far too big: his feet land on the Farmer’s shoulders, and the servants think their master is in danger.
evidence: putting his feet upon the Farmer’s shoulder attempted to climb into his lap

questions.prompt: The Farmer laughs before the servants come. How might his laughing have made the Ass go further?
facilitatorNotes: The Ass may think laughter means the Farmer likes it. Others may say the Ass did not notice the Farmer at all. Both can be argued from the order of events.
evidence: The Farmer could not hold his sides with laughter

readings.title: The Lion and the Mouse
readings.challenge: Connect the beginning and the end: a promise made early is kept later.
readings.focus: A small creature’s offer sounds silly until it comes true.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. To “do you a turn” is to do you a favour. A plight is a bad situation.

excerpt.locator: “The Lion and the Mouse,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “Once when a Lion was asleep a little Mouse began running up and down upon him; this soon…”; closes “Little friends may prove great friends.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Lion let the Mouse go?
facilitatorNotes: He is “tickled,” amused, by the idea of a mouse helping him. Ask whether he is being kind or just laughing.
evidence: The Lion was so tickled at the idea of the Mouse being able to help him

questions.prompt: What does the Mouse promise, and how does it keep the promise?
facilitatorNotes: To do the Lion a turn some day; later it gnaws through the hunters’ ropes.
evidence: who knows but what I may be able to do you a turn some of these days?
gnawed away the ropes

questions.prompt: Why can the little Mouse do what the huge Lion cannot?
facilitatorNotes: Strength is no use when you are tied; small sharp teeth are. The story turns size upside down.
evidence: the ropes that bound the King of the Beasts

questions.prompt: How do you think the Mouse says “Was I not right?” How might the Lion feel hearing it?
facilitatorNotes: Proud, cheerful, perhaps teasing; the Lion may feel thankful or a little foolish. Try two voices and compare.
evidence: Was I not right?

readings.title: The Swallow and the Other Birds
readings.challenge: Follow a chain of changes from a tiny seed to a trap.
readings.focus: A warning ignored while the danger is still small.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Hemp is a plant whose stems are made into strong string and rope. “Quoth” means said. To repent is to be sorry afterwards.

excerpt.locator: “The Swallow and the Other Birds,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “It happened that a Countryman was sowing some hemp seeds in a field where a Swallow and…”; closes “Destroy the seed of evil, or it will grow up to your ruin.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Swallow tell the other birds to do?
facilitatorNotes: Pick up every one of the hemp seeds before they can grow.
evidence: be careful to pick up every one of the seeds

questions.prompt: Retell the chain from seed to net.
facilitatorNotes: Seeds grow into hemp, hemp is made into cord, cord into nets, and the nets catch birds. Count the steps on fingers.
evidence: the hemp grew up and was made into cord, and of the cords nets were made

questions.prompt: Why might the birds have ignored the warning?
facilitatorNotes: A seed looks harmless and the danger is far off. Accept other reasons, such as not trusting the Swallow.
evidence: The birds paid no heed to the Swallow’s words

questions.prompt: The moral talks about “the seed of evil.” What could be a small seed of trouble in a person’s life?
facilitatorNotes: A little lie, an unkind habit, a small mess left to grow. The moral asks us to deal with trouble while it is small.
evidence: Destroy the seed of evil, or it will grow up to your ruin.

readings.title: The Frogs Desiring a King
readings.challenge: Compare the two kings the Frogs receive and how they treat each one.
readings.focus: Wishing to be ruled, and getting more than was wished for.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Jove is the king of the gods in old Roman stories. A petition is a request. A constitution is a set of rules for how a group is run. A stork is a large wading bird that eats frogs.

excerpt.locator: “The Frogs Desiring a King,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “The Frogs were living as happy as could be in a marshy swamp that just suited them; they…”; closes “Better no rule than cruel rule.”.

questions.prompt: How were the Frogs living before they asked for a king?
facilitatorNotes: Happily, in a swamp that suited them, with nobody bothering them. Hold on to this for the end.
evidence: living as happy as could be in a marshy swamp that just suited them

questions.prompt: How do the Frogs feel about King Log at first, and how do they treat him later?
facilitatorNotes: First terrified, then bolder, until they dance on him and ignore him.
evidence: frightened out of their lives
commenced dancing up and down upon it

questions.prompt: What do the Frogs mean by “a real king,” and what do they get?
facilitatorNotes: One who will truly rule them; they get a Stork that eats them. They got what they asked for, in a way they did not expect.
evidence: We want a real king; one that will really rule over us.

questions.prompt: Was Jove fair to the Frogs? Use the moral in your answer.
facilitatorNotes: Some children will say he punished them for being ungrateful; others that he only gave them what they asked. The moral, “Better no rule than cruel rule,” says the quiet log was the better king.
evidence: Better no rule than cruel rule.

readings.title: The Wolf and the Kid
readings.challenge: Notice where each animal is standing, and why that matters.
readings.focus: Bravery that depends on being out of reach.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A kid is a young goat. To revile someone is to shout insults at them.

excerpt.locator: “The Wolf and the Kid,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Kid was perched up on the top of a house, and looking down saw a Wolf passing under…”; closes ““It is easy to be brave from a safe distance.””.

questions.prompt: Where is the Kid, and where is the Wolf?
facilitatorNotes: The Kid is on top of a house; the Wolf is passing underneath, where he cannot reach.
evidence: perched up on the top of a house

questions.prompt: What does the Kid call the Wolf?
facilitatorNotes: “Murderer and thief.” Ask whether the Kid would say that standing next to him.
evidence: Murderer and thief

questions.prompt: Why doesn’t the Wolf seem angry?
facilitatorNotes: He knows the Kid only dares because he is safe up high. Some children may think the Wolf will wait for the Kid to come down.
evidence: Curse away, my young friend

questions.prompt: Is the Kid brave? Use the moral to explain.
facilitatorNotes: The Wolf says it is easy to be brave from a safe distance, so this is not real bravery. A child may point out that the Kid’s words are true; true words can still be said for show.
evidence: It is easy to be brave from a safe distance.

readings.title: The Woodman and the Serpent
readings.challenge: Follow what the Woodman does for the snake and what the snake does in return.
readings.focus: Kindness repaid with danger.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A serpent is a snake. A bosom is a person’s chest, here inside a coat. A hearth is the floor in front of a fireplace.
readings.contentNote: A snake nearly bites a child, and the Woodman kills it with his axe.

excerpt.locator: “The Woodman and the Serpent,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “One wintry day a Woodman was tramping home from his work when he saw something black…”; closes ““No gratitude from the wicked.””.

questions.prompt: Why does the Woodman think the Serpent is dead?
facilitatorNotes: It lies still in the snow and looks dead; “to all appearance” means it only looked that way.
evidence: to all appearance dead

questions.prompt: What kind things does the Woodman do for the Serpent?
facilitatorNotes: He carries it home inside his coat to warm it and lays it by the fire.
evidence: put it in his bosom to warm
put the Serpent down on the hearth before the fire

questions.prompt: What is the Serpent about to do when it wakes, and who is in danger?
facilitatorNotes: It raises its head to sting one of the children, the very child who reached out to stroke it.
evidence: about to sting the child to death

questions.prompt: The moral says, “No gratitude from the wicked.” Is the Serpent wicked, or just being a snake?
facilitatorNotes: The fable calls it wicked. Some children will say a cold, frightened snake bites whoever is near. Both views can use the story; ask what the Woodman should learn either way.
evidence: No gratitude from the wicked.

readings.title: The Jay and the Peacock
readings.challenge: Notice that the Jay ends up unwelcome in two places, not one.
readings.focus: Pretending to be what you are not.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A jay is a noisy bird with plain feathers; a peacock has a long, shining tail. Moulting is losing old feathers so new ones can grow. Plumes are feathers.

excerpt.locator: “The Jay and the Peacock,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Jay venturing into a yard where Peacocks used to walk, found there a number of feathers…”; closes ““It is not only fine feathers that make fine birds.””.

questions.prompt: Where does the Jay get the peacock feathers?
facilitatorNotes: From the yard, where the Peacocks had dropped them while moulting. He did not grow them; he found them.
evidence: feathers which had fallen from the Peacocks when they were moulting

questions.prompt: What do the Peacocks do when they see him?
facilitatorNotes: They see through the trick, peck him, and pull off the “borrowed plumes.”
evidence: they soon discovered the cheat
plucked away his borrowed plumes

questions.prompt: Why are the other Jays annoyed too, when he did nothing to them?
facilitatorNotes: He tried to leave them for something grander, and they watched it all. Some children may say they are embarrassed for him. Ask what “It is not only fine feathers that make fine birds” would mean coming from them.
evidence: they were equally annoyed with him
It is not only fine feathers that make fine birds.

readings.title: The Frog and the Ox
readings.challenge: Hear how repetition builds toward a sudden ending.
readings.focus: Refusing to admit that someone else is bigger.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. An ox is a big farm animal, a kind of cattle with horns. “Tush” means “nonsense.” Self-conceit is thinking too much of yourself.
readings.contentNote: The old Frog bursts at the end.

excerpt.locator: “The Frog and the Ox,” the whole fable with its moral; opens ““Oh Father,” said a little Frog to the big one sitting by the side of a pool, “I have…”; closes “Self-conceit may lead to self-destruction.”.

questions.prompt: How does the little Frog describe the Ox? Why does it sound like a monster?
facilitatorNotes: As big as a mountain, with horns, a tail and split hoofs. The little Frog has never seen an ox, so everything about it is strange.
evidence: It was as big as a mountain

questions.prompt: Count how many times the old Frog blows himself out. How does the writer make us feel it getting bigger?
facilitatorNotes: Three times, and each time the words repeat: “blew himself out” three times, then “blew and blew and blew, and swelled and swelled and swelled.” Read it aloud and puff up with it.
evidence: So he blew himself out, and blew himself out, and blew himself out.
blew and blew and blew, and swelled and swelled and swelled

questions.prompt: Why won’t the old Frog just say the Ox is bigger?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot bear to be smaller in front of his child; the moral calls it self-conceit. Some children may think he wanted to calm the little Frog’s fear; the words “I could easily make myself quite as broad” support boasting more.
evidence: I could easily make myself quite as broad
Self-conceit may lead to self-destruction.

readings.title: Androcles
readings.challenge: Remember a kindness from the beginning of the story when the danger comes at the end.
readings.focus: A wild animal’s gratitude saves the man who helped it.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. In ancient Rome some people were slaves, owned by others and forced to work; Androcles has run away. An arena was a great open space where crowds watched shows, sometimes cruel ones. To fawn is to act like a loving dog. Pardoned means let off a punishment.
readings.contentNote: Androcles is an enslaved man, and he is sentenced to be thrown to a hungry lion as a punishment. The lion does not harm him.

excerpt.locator: “Androcles,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A slave named Androcles once escaped from his master and fled to the forest. As he was…”; closes “Gratitude is the sign of noble souls.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Androcles turn back instead of running away from the Lion?
facilitatorNotes: The Lion does not chase him, and it is moaning in pain.
evidence: finding that the Lion did not pursue him

questions.prompt: What does Androcles do for the Lion, and what does the Lion do for him afterwards?
facilitatorNotes: He pulls out the thorn and binds the paw; the Lion takes him to its cave and brings him meat every day.
evidence: He pulled out the thorn and bound up the paw of the Lion
every day used to bring him meat

questions.prompt: In the arena the Lion rushes at Androcles “bounding and roaring.” What changes when he comes near?
facilitatorNotes: He recognises his friend and licks his hands like a friendly dog. The story uses the dog comparison twice: once in the forest and once in the arena.
evidence: he recognised his friend
licked his hands like a friendly dog

questions.prompt: The moral says, “Gratitude is the sign of noble souls.” Who in the story has a noble soul?
facilitatorNotes: The Lion, for remembering, and Androcles, for helping first. Some children will add the Emperor for setting them free. Ask for a reason from the story for each.
evidence: Gratitude is the sign of noble souls.
the slave was pardoned and freed

readings.title: The Bat, the Birds, and the Beasts
readings.challenge: Notice what the Bat answers each time someone asks him to join, and why his answer changes.
readings.focus: A creature who tries to belong to both sides ends up belonging to neither.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A bat has fur like a beast and wings like a bird, so the fable can make him either one. A conflict is a fight, and the armies are the two sides getting ready for it. To hesitate is to wait because you cannot decide; rejoicings are celebrations.

excerpt.locator: “The Bat, the Birds, and the Beasts,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A great conflict was about to come off between the Birds and the Beasts. When the two…”; closes ““He that is neither one thing nor the other has no friends.””.

questions.prompt: What does the Bat tell the Birds, and what does he tell the Beasts?
facilitatorNotes: To the Birds he says he is a Beast; to the Beasts he says he is a Bird. Either way, he does not join.
evidence: I am a Beast.
I am a Bird.

questions.prompt: Why does the Bat keep giving these answers before the battle?
facilitatorNotes: He does not want to choose, perhaps because he is afraid of the fight or wants to wait and see who wins. Some children will say he really is a bit of both, which is what makes his answers sound true.
evidence: the Bat hesitated which to join

questions.prompt: When peace is made, the Bat wants to join the celebrations. Why do both sides send him away?
facilitatorNotes: He would not stand with either side when it was dangerous, so neither side trusts him now. He wanted the party without the danger.
evidence: they all turned against him and he had to fly away

questions.prompt: The Bat says, “He that is neither one thing nor the other has no friends.” Is it ever right not to take a side?
facilitatorNotes: Children may say yes, when both sides are fighting for a bad reason. The fable’s point is about changing your answer to please whoever is asking. Let both views be argued.
evidence: He that is neither one thing nor the other has no friends.

readings.title: The Hart and the Hunter
readings.challenge: Compare what the Hart loves about himself with what actually helps him.
readings.focus: The part he admired traps him, and the part he disliked nearly saved him.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A hart is a male deer, and his antlers are the branching horns on his head. Slim and slight means thin; nimble means quick and light. To despise something is to look down on it. “Alas!” is a cry of sorrow.
readings.contentNote: A hunter shoots an arrow at the deer, and the fable ends as he is caught.

excerpt.locator: “The Hart and the Hunter,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “The Hart was once drinking from a pool and admiring the noble figure he made there. “Ah,”…”; closes ““We often despise what is most useful to us.””.

questions.prompt: Looking into the pool, what does the Hart admire, and what does he wish were different?
facilitatorNotes: He admires his antlers and wishes his legs were not so thin.
evidence: it is a pity they are so slim and slight

questions.prompt: When the Hunter comes, which part of the Hart helps him, and which part gets him caught?
facilitatorNotes: His quick legs carry him nearly out of sight; his antlers catch in the low branches.
evidence: by the aid of his nimble legs
his antlers were caught

questions.prompt: The Hart calls his antlers a “noble crown.” What does the word crown tell you about how he sees himself?
facilitatorNotes: Like a king, very proud and grand. A crown is for show, which is part of the fable’s point.
evidence: such a noble crown

questions.prompt: Say the moral in your own words. What did the Hart learn too late?
facilitatorNotes: That the plain thing he looked down on, his legs, was the most useful, and the beautiful thing he loved trapped him.
evidence: We often despise what is most useful to us.

readings.title: The Man and the Wood
readings.challenge: Work out what the Man’s “particular purpose” is before the Trees do.
readings.focus: Kind trees give away the one thing their enemy needed.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. An axe has a metal head for cutting and a wooden handle to swing it by; the head alone cannot chop a tree. Good-natured means kind and ready to help.

excerpt.locator: “The Man and the Wood,” the whole fable; opens “A Man came into a Wood one day with an axe in his hand, and begged all the Trees to give…”; closes “…saw how foolish they had been in giving their enemy the means of destroying themselves.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Man ask the Trees for? Does he tell them why he wants it?
facilitatorNotes: One small branch. He says only that it is for “a particular purpose,” and does not say what.
evidence: which he wanted for a particular purpose

questions.prompt: What does the Man do with the branch, and what happens next?
facilitatorNotes: He fits it into his axe head as a handle and cuts down tree after tree.
evidence: fix it into the axe head

questions.prompt: The Trees were good-natured. Was it wrong to be kind? What could they have done instead?
facilitatorNotes: Being kind was not wrong, but they could have asked what the branch was for. Some children will say the Trees could not have known; the fable calls them foolish all the same. Both are fair.
evidence: the Trees saw how foolish they had been in giving their enemy the means of destroying themselves

readings.title: The Dog and the Wolf
readings.challenge: Listen for the small sign the Wolf notices on the way to town.
readings.focus: A hungry wolf chooses freedom over a full dish.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Gaunt means very thin from hunger. A place here means a job. At night the Dog wears a collar on a chain; to chafe is to rub sore. A slave is a person who is not free.

excerpt.locator: “The Dog and the Wolf,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A gaunt Wolf was almost dead with hunger when he happened to meet a House-dog who was…”; closes “Better starve free than be a fat slave.”.

questions.prompt: How are the Dog and the Wolf different when they meet?
facilitatorNotes: The Dog is well fed and gets his food regularly; the Wolf is almost dead with hunger.
evidence: A gaunt Wolf was almost dead with hunger

questions.prompt: What does the Wolf notice on the Dog’s neck? How does the Dog explain it?
facilitatorNotes: The hair is worn away where the collar goes on at night. The Dog says it rubs a little but you get used to it.
evidence: it chafes a bit, but one soon gets used to it

questions.prompt: The Dog says, “Oh, it is nothing.” Do you think it is really nothing?
facilitatorNotes: Not to the Wolf: the worn neck means being chained up every night. Some children will agree with the Dog that a little rubbing is worth a warm home.
evidence: Oh, it is nothing

questions.prompt: Why does the Wolf say good-bye? Would you have gone with the Dog?
facilitatorNotes: He would rather be hungry and free than fed and chained. Many children will choose food and a home; that is a fair answer, and worth comparing with the moral.
evidence: Better starve free than be a fat slave.

readings.title: The Belly and the Members
readings.challenge: Follow what happens to each part of the body when the others stop working.
readings.focus: Quiet work is still needed work, and a body, or a group, works only together.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Here the Members are the parts of the body, such as the hands, mouth, teeth and legs, and the Belly is the stomach. To strike work is to stop working until you get what you want. Parched means very dry.

excerpt.locator: “The Belly and the Members,” the whole fable; opens “One fine day it occurred to the Members of the Body that they were doing all the work and…”; closes “…work for the Body, and that all must work together or the Body will go to pieces.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the Hands, Mouth and Teeth angry with the Belly?
facilitatorNotes: They think they do all the work while the Belly gets all the food.
evidence: they were doing all the work and the Belly was having all the food

questions.prompt: What happens to the Hands, the Mouth and the Legs after a day or two?
facilitatorNotes: The Hands can hardly move, the Mouth is dry, and the Legs cannot hold the body up.
evidence: the Hands could hardly move, and the Mouth was all parched and dry

questions.prompt: What was the Belly doing all along, in its “dull quiet way”?
facilitatorNotes: Turning food into the strength the whole body needs. Its work was hard to see, but necessary.
evidence: even the Belly in its dull quiet way was doing necessary work for the Body

questions.prompt: This fable is really about people. Who in a family or a class might be like the Belly?
facilitatorNotes: Someone whose work is quiet and easy to miss, such as the person who cooks or tidies. Accept any answer that explains why everyone needs that work.
evidence: all must work together or the Body will go to pieces

readings.title: The Fox and the Grapes; The Peacock and Juno
readings.challenge: Hear two short fables about wanting something you cannot have, and compare the two animals.
readings.focus: One animal pretends he never wanted the grapes; the other is told to be content with what he has.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A vine is a climbing plant, and lofty means high up. To quench your thirst is to stop being thirsty; quoth means said. In old Roman stories Juno was the queen of the gods and the peacock was her bird. A petition is a request, a nightingale is a small bird with a beautiful song, and your lot is what you have been given.

excerpt.locator: “The Fox and the Grapes” and “The Peacock and Juno,” two whole fables with their morals; opens “One hot summer’s day a Fox was strolling through an orchard till he came to a bunch of…”; closes ““Be content with your lot; one cannot be first in everything.””.

questions.prompt: How many times does the Fox try for the grapes? Show how he jumps.
facilitatorNotes: Again and again: a run and a jump, then “One, Two, Three,” then more tries until he gives up.
evidence: Turning round again with a One, Two, Three, he jumped up

questions.prompt: Why does the Fox say the grapes are sour? Does he know they are?
facilitatorNotes: He never tasted them. He says it so that losing them does not seem to matter, and his nose in the air hides his disappointment.
evidence: walked away with his nose in the air
I am sure they are sour.

questions.prompt: What does the Peacock ask Juno for, and what does he already have?
facilitatorNotes: A nightingale’s voice, on top of his beautiful feathers; and he is already her favourite bird.
evidence: the voice of a nightingale in addition to his other attractions

questions.prompt: Both animals cannot have what they want. Who handles it better, or do both need Juno’s advice?
facilitatorNotes: The Fox pretends he never wanted it; the Peacock keeps asking. Juno’s “Be content with your lot” could fit them both. Accept any answer that compares what they do.
evidence: It is easy to despise what you cannot get.
one cannot be first in everything

readings.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
readings.challenge: Compare one summer day for the Ant and for the Grasshopper, then see what winter brings.
readings.focus: Getting ready for hard times, and the question of whether to share.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. An ear of corn is the part of the plant where the grain grows. Toiling and moiling means working very hard. Necessity means real need. (This text has no opening quotation mark before “we have got plenty”; the Grasshopper is still speaking.)
readings.contentNote: In winter the Grasshopper is dying of hunger.

excerpt.locator: “The Ant and the Grasshopper,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “In a field one summer’s day a Grasshopper was hopping about, chirping and singing to its…”; closes “It is best to prepare for the days of necessity.”.

questions.prompt: What is the Grasshopper doing on the summer day, and what is the Ant doing?
facilitatorNotes: The Grasshopper hops, chirps and sings; the Ant carries an ear of corn to the nest with great effort.
evidence: chirping and singing to its heart’s content
bearing along with great toil an ear of corn

questions.prompt: What does the Grasshopper say about winter? Why is he wrong?
facilitatorNotes: “Why bother about winter?” He has plenty now, but summer food does not last and winter will come.
evidence: Why bother about winter?

questions.prompt: In winter the ants share out corn every day. Should they share with the Grasshopper?
facilitatorNotes: The fable does not say. Some children will say kindness means sharing; others that he must learn. Both can point to the words.
evidence: the ants distributing every day corn and grain from the stores they had collected in the summer

questions.prompt: Is the moral saying that singing and playing are bad?
facilitatorNotes: No: it says to get ready for days of need as well. The Grasshopper’s mistake was doing nothing else.
evidence: It is best to prepare for the days of necessity.

readings.title: The Fox and the Cat
readings.challenge: Count the tricks each animal has, then watch which ones work.
readings.focus: One sure plan beats a hundred clever ones when there is no time to choose.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. To boast is to brag. Devices here are clever plans. Hounds are hunting dogs, and huntsmen hunt with them. Miss Puss is an old pet name for a cat. To reckon on something is to count on it.
readings.contentNote: The hunting dogs catch the Fox, and the huntsmen kill him.

excerpt.locator: “The Fox and the Cat,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Fox was boasting to a Cat of its clever devices for escaping its enemies. “I have a…”; closes ““Better one safe way than a hundred on which you cannot reckon.””.

questions.prompt: How many tricks does the Fox say he has? How many does the Cat have?
facilitatorNotes: The Fox has a whole bag, a hundred ways of escaping; the Cat has only one.
evidence: I have a whole bag of tricks
I have only one

questions.prompt: What is the Cat’s one trick? Why does it work?
facilitatorNotes: She runs straight up a tree and hides. She does not need to think, so she is safe at once.
evidence: the Cat immediately scampered up a tree and hid herself in the boughs

questions.prompt: Why do the Fox’s hundred tricks not save him?
facilitatorNotes: He spends the time deciding which to use, and the hounds reach him while he is still thinking.
evidence: while he was debating the hounds came nearer and nearer

questions.prompt: Is it better to know one thing well or many things a little?
facilitatorNotes: The moral chooses one safe way. Some children will say many tricks are good if you choose fast; that is a fair answer to discuss.
evidence: Better one safe way than a hundred on which you cannot reckon.

readings.title: The Wolf in Sheep’s Clothing
readings.challenge: Notice why the Lamb follows the Wolf.
readings.focus: A disguise works because everyone trusts what they see.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Vigilance is careful watching. A pelt is an animal’s own skin and fur; flayed means skinned. Appearances are how things look from outside, and deceptive means they can trick you.
readings.contentNote: The Wolf leads a lamb away and eats her, and goes on eating sheep.

excerpt.locator: “The Wolf in Sheep’s Clothing,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Wolf found great difficulty in getting at the sheep owing to the vigilance of the…”; closes “Appearances are deceptive.”.

questions.prompt: Why can the Wolf not get at the sheep at the start?
facilitatorNotes: The shepherd and his dogs watch them carefully.
evidence: owing to the vigilance of the shepherd and his dogs

questions.prompt: How does the Wolf trick the sheep? Why does the Lamb follow him?
facilitatorNotes: He wears a sheep’s skin over his own. It was the skin of the Lamb’s own mother, so the Lamb follows what looks like her.
evidence: The Lamb that belonged to the sheep, whose skin the Wolf was wearing, began to follow the Wolf

questions.prompt: In this telling the Wolf is not caught. Why might the fable end that way?
facilitatorNotes: To show how well a disguise can work, so we are careful. Many children will want the Wolf caught; ask why the fable does not give them that.
evidence: for some time he succeeded in deceiving the sheep

questions.prompt: What does “Appearances are deceptive” mean for the sheep in this fable?
facilitatorNotes: What looked like a sheep was really a wolf; looking safe is not the same as being safe.
evidence: Appearances are deceptive.

readings.title: The Shepherd’s Boy
readings.challenge: Count how many times the boy calls “Wolf” and what happens each time.
readings.focus: A trick played for fun uses up the trust that he needs when trouble is real.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A shepherd looks after sheep, and to tend them is to take care of them. To worry the sheep here means to chase and bite them. Villagers are the people who live in a village.
readings.contentNote: A wolf attacks the flock and eats the sheep.

excerpt.locator: “The Shepherd’s Boy,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “There was once a young Shepherd Boy who tended his sheep at the foot of a mountain near a…”; closes ““A liar will not be believed, even when he speaks the truth.””.

questions.prompt: Why does the Shepherd Boy first cry “Wolf”?
facilitatorNotes: He is lonely all day and wants company and excitement.
evidence: It was rather lonely for him all day

questions.prompt: What do the villagers do the first two times, and what do they do the third time?
facilitatorNotes: They run out and stay with him; the third time nobody comes, because they think he is tricking them again.
evidence: who had been fooled twice before

questions.prompt: When the Wolf really comes, the boy shouts louder than ever. Why does being louder not help?
facilitatorNotes: The trouble is not how loud he is but whether people believe him, and he has used up their trust.
evidence: still louder than before

questions.prompt: The boy was lonely. What could he have done instead of tricking people?
facilitatorNotes: Asked someone to keep him company, or told the truth about being lonely. Connect it to the wise man’s words.
evidence: A liar will not be believed, even when he speaks the truth.

readings.title: The Tortoise and the Birds
readings.challenge: Ask yourself whether the Tortoise picked a safe helper.
readings.focus: Trusting a helper who would gain from hurting you is dangerous.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A tortoise is a land turtle with a hard shell. Residence means home. Talons are a bird’s sharp claws, to soar aloft is to fly high, and pinions are wings.
readings.contentNote: The Eagle drops the Tortoise on a sharp rock and the two birds eat him.

excerpt.locator: “The Tortoise and the Birds,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Tortoise desired to change its place of residence, so he asked an Eagle to carry him to…”; closes “Never soar aloft on an enemy’s pinions.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Tortoise want, and how does he plan to get there?
facilitatorNotes: To move to a new home, carried by the Eagle, who is promised a reward.
evidence: he asked an Eagle to carry him to his new home

questions.prompt: What does the Crow say, and what does the Eagle do with the hint?
facilitatorNotes: That tortoise is good to eat and rocks will crack the shell; the Eagle drops him on a rock.
evidence: The rocks will soon crack the shell

questions.prompt: The Eagle agreed to help. Why does the moral call her an enemy?
facilitatorNotes: Eagles eat creatures like tortoises, so she could gain more by hurting him than by helping him. Some children will blame the Crow most; both birds share the meal.
evidence: Never soar aloft on an enemy’s pinions.

readings.title: The Two Fellows and the Bear
readings.challenge: Watch what each traveller does when the Bear comes, and what that shows.
readings.focus: A friend who leaves you in danger is told the truth in a clever way.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Fellows here are two men travelling together. A muzzle is an animal’s nose and mouth. Master Bruin is an old storybook name for a bear. At a pinch means in trouble, and to desert is to run off and leave someone.

excerpt.locator: “The Two Fellows and the Bear,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “Two Fellows were travelling together through a wood, when a Bear rushed out upon them.…”; closes ““Never trust a friend who deserts you at a pinch.””.

questions.prompt: What does each traveller do when the Bear rushes out?
facilitatorNotes: The one in front climbs a tree and hides; the other lies flat with his face in the dust.
evidence: he seized hold of the branch of a tree, and hid himself among the leaves
threw himself flat down upon the ground

questions.prompt: Why does the Bear go away?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks the man is dead, and the fable says bears will not touch dead meat. That is an old belief, not a fact: real bears sometimes do eat dead animals.
evidence: for bears will not touch dead meat

questions.prompt: Did the Bear really whisper something? Why does the man say it did?
facilitatorNotes: No. It is a clever way to tell his friend what he thinks of him without saying it straight out.
evidence: What was it that Master Bruin whispered to you?
Never trust a friend who deserts you at a pinch.

questions.prompt: The man in the tree comes down laughing. What does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He does not seem sorry or ashamed; he treats his friend’s danger as a joke. Some children will say he is laughing from relief; ask whether he says sorry.
evidence: laughing, said

readings.title: The Two Pots
readings.challenge: Work out which pot is strong and which is weak, and why that matters.
readings.focus: Good intentions cannot make a fragile thing safe beside a hard one.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Brass is a hard metal. Earthenware is pottery of baked clay, which breaks easily. The tide is water rising, aloof means keeping apart, and in contact means touching.

excerpt.locator: “The Two Pots,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “Two Pots had been left on the bank of a river, one of brass, and one of earthenware. When…”; closes “The strong and the weak cannot keep company.”.

questions.prompt: Which pot is strong and which is weak? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: The brass pot is strong and the earthenware pot is weak, because clay breaks and metal does not. The earthenware pot keeps away.
evidence: one of brass, and one of earthenware

questions.prompt: The brass pot promises not to hit. Why is the earthenware pot still afraid?
facilitatorNotes: Any bump will break it, whichever pot does the bumping.
evidence: whether I hit you, or you hit me, I shall suffer for it

questions.prompt: Is the brass pot kind? Does its kindness help?
facilitatorNotes: It means well, but kind words cannot change what the pots are made of. Some children will say the strong pot should just be careful; the moral says they cannot keep company. Let them disagree.
evidence: Fear nothing, friend, I will not strike you.
The strong and the weak cannot keep company.

readings.title: The Four Oxen and the Lion
readings.challenge: Picture how the Oxen stand together, and then how they stand apart.
readings.focus: Together they are safe; a quarrel splits them and the Lion wins.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. Oxen are big cattle (one ox, two oxen). To prowl is to creep about hunting. Pasture is a grassy field for grazing. United means together, and divided means apart.
readings.contentNote: The Lion kills the four oxen one by one.

excerpt.locator: “The Four Oxen and the Lion,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Lion used to prowl about a field in which Four Oxen used to dwell. Many a time he tried…”; closes “United we stand, divided we fall.”.

questions.prompt: How do the Four Oxen keep the Lion away? Show it with four fingers.
facilitatorNotes: They stand tail to tail, so wherever the Lion comes he meets a pair of horns.
evidence: they turned their tails to one another

questions.prompt: What changes, and what happens then?
facilitatorNotes: They quarrel and each grazes alone in a different corner, so the Lion can attack them one at a time.
evidence: they fell a-quarrelling among themselves
each went off to pasture alone in a separate corner of the field

questions.prompt: What do you think the Oxen quarrelled about? Why does the fable not tell us?
facilitatorNotes: We are not told; it does not matter what the quarrel was, only that it split them. Children may invent reasons.
evidence: they fell a-quarrelling among themselves

questions.prompt: What does “United we stand, divided we fall” mean?
facilitatorNotes: Together we stay safe and strong; apart, each one can be beaten.
evidence: United we stand, divided we fall.

readings.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
readings.challenge: Join in each time the pebble sentence comes round.
readings.focus: Patience and a good idea solve a problem that force could not.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A pitcher is a tall jug with a narrow mouth. In despair means giving up hope. A pebble is a small stone.

excerpt.locator: “The Crow and the Pitcher,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Crow, half-dead with thirst, came upon a Pitcher which had once been full of water; but…”; closes “Little by little does the trick.”.

questions.prompt: What is the Crow’s problem?
facilitatorNotes: He is very thirsty, and the little water left in the pitcher is too low for his beak.
evidence: he could not reach far enough down to get at it

questions.prompt: Say the pebble sentence with me each time it comes. How many pebbles does it take?
facilitatorNotes: Six are told one by one, and then “a few more.” The repeating makes us feel how long and patient the work is.
evidence: Then he took another pebble and dropped it into the Pitcher.

questions.prompt: Why does the water rise when the Crow drops in pebbles? Try it with a glass of water and some stones.
facilitatorNotes: The stones take up room at the bottom and push the water up. Scientists have seen some real crows and rooks solve a puzzle like this.
evidence: he saw the water mount up near him

questions.prompt: “Little by little does the trick.” What would have happened if the Crow had given up after two pebbles?
facilitatorNotes: He would still be thirsty; only many small steps raised the water. Children may give examples of their own.
evidence: Little by little does the trick.

readings.title: The Goose With the Golden Eggs
readings.challenge: Notice how the countryman changes as he gets rich.
readings.focus: Wanting everything at once loses even what you had.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A countryman lives on a farm. As heavy as lead means very heavy. Greedy means always wanting more. “Greed oft o’er reaches itself” means greed often reaches too far.

excerpt.locator: “The Goose With the Golden Eggs,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “One day a countryman going to the nest of his Goose found there an egg all yellow and…”; closes “Greed oft o’er reaches itself.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the man almost throw the first egg away?
facilitatorNotes: It is as heavy as lead, and he thinks someone is playing a trick on him.
evidence: he thought a trick had been played upon him

questions.prompt: How does the man change as he gets rich?
facilitatorNotes: He grows greedy.
evidence: As he grew rich he grew greedy

questions.prompt: Why does he kill the Goose, and what does he find?
facilitatorNotes: He wants all the gold at once, but there is nothing inside, and now there will be no more eggs.
evidence: thinking to get at once all the gold the Goose could give

questions.prompt: If he had been patient, what would he have had?
facilitatorNotes: A golden egg every morning, for as long as the Goose lived.
evidence: Every morning the same thing occurred

readings.title: The Wind and the Sun
readings.challenge: Watch what the traveller does with his cloak each time.
readings.focus: Gentle warmth does what force cannot.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. To dispute is to argue. A cloak is a loose coat without sleeves. Kindness effects more than severity means that gentleness gets more done than harshness.

excerpt.locator: “The Wind and the Sun,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “The Wind and the Sun were disputing which was the stronger. Suddenly they saw a traveller…”; closes “Kindness effects more than severity.”.

questions.prompt: How do the Wind and the Sun decide which is stronger?
facilitatorNotes: Whichever can make the traveller take off his cloak wins.
evidence: Whichever of us can cause that traveller to take off his cloak shall be regarded as the stronger

questions.prompt: What happens the harder the Wind blows?
facilitatorNotes: The traveller wraps his cloak more tightly around him.
evidence: the harder he blew the more closely did the traveller wrap his cloak round him

questions.prompt: The Sun lets the Wind go first. Why might the Sun do that?
facilitatorNotes: Perhaps the Sun already knows blowing will fail and wants the Wind to see it; or it is simply polite. Both fit.
evidence: You begin.

questions.prompt: When might a gentle way work better than a rough one?
facilitatorNotes: Like the traveller, people often hold on tighter when pushed and give way when treated warmly. Accept examples tied to the story.
evidence: Kindness effects more than severity.

readings.title: The Man, the Boy, and the Donkey
readings.challenge: Keep a list of everyone who tells the Man what to do.
readings.focus: Trying to please everyone ends in a plan that pleases no one.
readings.context: From Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 retelling of Aesop’s fables, very old stories that end with a lesson called the moral. A market is where people buy and sell. A lout is a rude, clumsy fellow, and to trudge is to walk heavily. To jeer and to scoff are to make fun of someone. Hulking means big and heavy.
readings.contentNote: The donkey falls off a bridge and drowns.

excerpt.locator: “The Man, the Boy, and the Donkey,” the whole fable with its moral; opens “A Man and his son were once going with their Donkey to market. As they were walking along…”; closes ““Please all, and you will please none.””.

questions.prompt: Who tells the Man what to do along the road? What does the first one say?
facilitatorNotes: A countryman, a group of men, two women, and people in the town. The countryman says a donkey is for riding.
evidence: what is a Donkey for but to ride upon?

questions.prompt: Each time someone speaks, what does the Man change?
facilitatorNotes: First the Boy rides, then the Man rides, then both ride, and at last they carry the Donkey.
evidence: So the Man put the Boy on the Donkey

questions.prompt: Carrying the Donkey on a pole is the silliest plan of all. How did the Man end up there?
facilitatorNotes: He kept changing to please whoever spoke last, until nothing sensible was left.
evidence: They thought and they thought, till at last they cut down a pole

questions.prompt: What should the Man have done? What does the old man mean?
facilitatorNotes: Decided for himself what was sensible, perhaps walking as they began. You cannot please everyone, and trying pleases no one.
evidence: Please all, and you will please none.
